lesson.title: Dates & Appointments

hook.title: How Spanish Builds Any Date: 'El [Number] de [Month]'
hook.content: You already know the most famous date formula in Spanish: el cinco de mayo ('the fifth of May')! Unlike English, which uses ordinal numbers ('the fifth, the tenth, the twentieth'), Spanish uses regular cardinal numbers for every day of the month from 2 to 31: el dos de enero ('January 2nd'), el diez de enero ('January 10th'), el veinte de enero ('January 20th')!

pattern.title: Months Take 'En'; Specific Dates Take 'El'
pattern.content: Compare: En enero ('In January') vs El cinco de enero ('On January 5th').

enero.etymology_derivation: Months take en ('in'): en enero, en mayo.

lunes.etymology_derivation: Spanish uses the masculine article el/los to mean 'on [weekday]': el lunes ('on Monday'), los lunes ('on Mondays')!

martes.context_translation: We'll see each other on Tuesday.

semana.context_translation: This week I have a lot of work.

de.context_translation: I am coming from the hotel.
de.etymology_derivation: Fuses with masculine singular article el into del ('of the / from the').

en.context_phrase: Vivo en Madrid y el libro está en la mesa.
en.context_translation: I live in Madrid and the book is on the table.
en.etymology_derivation: One Spanish preposition covers 'in' (en la casa), 'on' (en la mesa), and 'at' (en el hotel)!

el.etymology_derivation: Latin demonstrative ille ('that one') trimmed down over centuries to el. Spanish pointers became articles.
